title: Hattie and the Sparkle Thief
markdown:
Dawn broke. Colours arrived in a rush. Inside Hattie the hamster’s burrow, a tiny heart thumped. Today was the science fair. The prize rocket, the Stardust Sprinter, promised distant galaxies. Hattie twitched her whiskers. A thrill bounced from toes to tail.

Hattie adored sparkle. Her burrow overflowed with the sparkliest fluffiest bedding. It shimmered. But big events? Crowds? A shiver jolted her. Paws wobbled. Voice squeaked. She hoped nobody noticed the shy tremor.

Caper the alley cat’s workshop buzzed. Whizz. Bang. Clatter. Caper, a sleek black inventor with emerald eyes, built ingenious contraptions from bits and bobs. He bounced. “The Stardust Sprinter,” he declared, tail a happy decisive flick. “A magnificent machine.”

Suddenly, a hush. Mrs. Gable’s face paled. “Oh, no.” The Stardust Sprinter spot was empty. A single iridescent feather fluttered down, a tiny lost jewel.

“A thief,” Caper yowled. He spotted the feather. “Pipkin.” Pipkin, a pigeon with a taste for glitter and a habit of borrowing, had snatched it.

Hattie peeked out. Pipkin. Fast. Loud. The fair buzzed with people. Her shyness prickled. But Mrs. Gable looked sad. The rocket represented so much.

“Hattie.” Caper zoomed over. “Pipkin’s taken the rocket. Toward the park. I saw sparkle heading for the old oak.”

Hattie’s whiskers drooped. Wet streets. Splashy puddles. Distant traffic. Sticky heavy paws. The nervous wobble returned. She wanted to burrow. Stay hidden. But Mrs. Gable’s slumped shoulders. The rocket.

“I’ll help,” Hattie squeaked. The words surprised her. Her tummy did a somersaulting flip-flop.

“Brilliant,” Caper yipped. “A wet and wild chase.”

They burst into cool damp air. Drizzle made the pavement gleam. Hattie’s eyes darted, catching glints. Pipkin’s glitter trail sparkled like fallen stars. “This way.” Caper weaved around a gushing drainpipe, water spraying high.

They zipped past scowling trash cans. Ducked under dripping awnings. Hattie had to dash. Little legs pumped. Every loud splash, every sudden gust, tempted her back. She skidded near a narrow dark drainpipe. A shortcut? Terribly dark. Too small? Heart thumped faster. What if she got stuck? What if Pipkin waited? She almost froze.

“Come on, Hattie,” Caper echoed. “Pipkin wouldn’t fit, but a determined hamster like you? You’ve got this.”

Hattie took a deep breath and squeezed in. Rough damp metal scraped her fur. Breath hitched. Faint dripping. A damp earthy smell of forgotten things. An eternity of dark confined space. Then a glimmer. A final push, and she tumbled out, blinking onto damp cool grass.

Pipkin perched on a rickety fence. The Stardust Sprinter sat beside him. He looked wistful. Beside him a wobbly contraption of twigs and foil.

“Pipkin,” Caper boomed. “You took the rocket. What were you thinking?”

Pipkin blinked. “I just wanted to see the clouds. From up close. My contraption pushes air down. But it needs more spark. More shimmer.” He gestured sadly.

Hattie looked at his yearning. He wanted to fly. She looked at his contraption, then at her own sparkly bedding, her pride. Giving it away felt like losing a piece of herself. She imagined rough twigs and damp earth against the comforting ticklish sparkle. But Pipkin’s hopeful eyes held her. With a deep breath she nudged a pawful of beloved bedding toward him.

“I have some very sparkly bedding,” she said, voice clear and steady. “It’s the best. It might help your contraption really fly.”

Caper looked surprised. “Hattie, are you sure?”

She nodded. A tiny wobble remained, but determination bloomed. “It’s okay. It’s worth a try.”

With a flurry of Pipkin’s wings, a dash from Caper securing the rocket, and a determined scamper from Hattie, the Stardust Sprinter was retrieved. Hattie dug into her cheek pouches, familiar sparkle tickling whiskers, and offered a generous handful. Pipkin tucked it reverently into his contraption. “Thank you. Thank you so much.”

They raced back, Pipkin overhead, rocket in Caper’s paws, arriving just as parents entered. Mrs. Gable cried out with pure joy. Face beaming.

Hattie, damp but feeling dry inside, watched the happy hubbub. She hadn’t hidden. She hadn’t only squeaked. She had helped.

Later the sun broke through, orange and pink. A small contraption sputtered, lifted with a whoosh. Pipkin’s. It didn’t reach the clouds, not yet, but it lifted. Pipkin beamed. Hattie watched, a warm proud feeling spreading. Her shyness was a quiet hum. It didn’t stop her. She had shared her sparkle.

“Today,” she said, already bouncing toward the next experiment, “is going to be fantastic.”
